We have lived wholly off grid in a small cabin in the Deep South for 12 years. By design we have no A/C but don’t really need it. We use propane for cooking and wood with propane backup for heat. Our fridge runs off 12/24/110V. Our power usage is very modest. With all that being said, our evolving solar system has run about $12G to date. From our research for others wanting to wholly convert (which is virtually impossible if you are in any kind of city limits) a turnkey solar power system will run about $25-$30G in materials only. What we also found is that even in unincorporated areas and county residences, if power is available via a public utility, you are required to be grid tied. That means your batteries do not produce power for you when the grid goes down or is shut off.

Just have 2 parallel systems. Grid power and then solar. You have to have power and a meter, doesn't mean you have to use it for your whole house.

Used ~400w panels are under $200. The batteries are what really hurt. $12g buys a lot of solar if you're not paying someone to put it in.

Many utility companies will not allow parallel systems. Batteries are expensive. We looked at forklift batteries but just couldn’t swing $5G. Our $12G is over 12 years. We learned a LOT in upgrading. Like how not to fry $1G in batteries at one whack. Right now to outright purchase what we have would be about $3-4G. But if you want a system to run state of the art fridges and freezers, A/C, desktop PCs, gaming consoles, etc etc etc, you will need upwards of a $20G outlay, even if you install it yourself.

Simple solution to this is keep a UPS on hand. When power goes out, turn off the main and cut off a power cord, plug it into the ups and back feed it into a 10 amp breaker (Important so you don't draw too much power from it). Boom.. your grid tie system thinks its connected to the grid again and starts producing power.

They call it a safety feature.. lol.. So here's how it works.. the solar panels produce energy and it goes to an inverter that converts it from dc to ac. That inverter only stays powered on and converting energy as long as it sees power coming from the grid. As soon as the grid stops producing power, the inverter shuts off and stops converting dc to ac. The claim is it prevents someone working on the down lines from being electrocuted.. They could simply add an automatic shut off that disconnects the main from your house when the grid goes down.. but this adds cost so its not done. You can also get a back up battery and use that to feed ac back into the inverter once the main is shut off.. This is a pretty simple solution and easy to do to keep your solar panels producing power without the grid being up.
